parts.title: Predicting which bank customers will stay, using a combined AI model (SVC-SDNN) to help banks look after their customers
parts.abstract:
Many problems in banks and other businesses can be solved with clever, creative ideas that use artificial intelligence (AI). Every bank needs AI tools that spot "churn", meaning customers who are likely to leave, so that it can look after its customers better. This is part of what is called customer relationship management (CRM). To predict churn well on a dataset that anyone can download, we suggest a new combined AI method. It also works efficiently on any private, hidden bank dataset, as long as the data is arranged in the right format. We compared our method with other combined methods.

We searched carefully for the best smart solution. We found that joining a Sequential Deep Neural Network (SDNN) with a Support Vector Machine (SVM) gives excellent predictions. We judged this with four scores: accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score. It is essential to correctly identify the important factors, or the things that cause churn. Our combined model, SVC-SDNN, is strong at predicting which customers are most likely to leave, and at finding the key factors that affect whether customers stay. Our approach reached an AUC-ROC score of 0.881696 and an accuracy of 0.95.
parts.introduction_first:
Keeping customers is directly linked to how profitable and successful a business is. Customer Relationship Management (CRM) is a planned way of working that helps a business keep track of, and judge, how customers interact with it and what information it holds about them, from the first contact all the way through. The main aim of CRM is to make customers happier and more loyal, so that more of them stay.

Two advanced machine learning methods can be used to make predictions like this [1]. A machine learning method is a computer program that learns patterns from examples. The first is the Support Vector Classifier (SVC). The second is the Sequential Deep Neural Network (SDNN), a type of neural network, which is a computer system loosely inspired by the brain. SDNNs can handle complicated data, spot complicated patterns and notice new trends that ordinary analysis methods might miss. With SDNNs, banks can make more accurate predictions about how customers behave, including whether they will stay.

Several studies have used neural networks to predict whether customers will stay. They focused on predicting churn in different industries, using various machine learning models.

Saran Kumar and Chandrakala (2016) [2] found that support vector machines work very well at sorting things into groups. This is because they draw a simple dividing line between groups, they work well on new data they have not seen before, and they fit the data very precisely. They tested a churn prediction model called EBURM [3]. It runs on online shops and can give each customer personalized recommendations. This is different from the usual recommendation systems, which suggest things based on the content of products or on what other people bought.

De Caigny et al. (2018) [1] concluded that a linear logistic model, a simple statistical model, performs well overall at prediction. Sabbeh (2018) [4] showed that ensemble models, which combine the answers of many smaller models, such as random forest and ad-boost, perform well at predicting churn. Kaur [5] found that random forest works better than other machine learning methods. Leung and Chung (2020) [6] predicted churn by fine-tuning particular models. Domingos et al. (2021) [7] used hyper-tuning, which means carefully adjusting a model's settings, on existing models for the banking industry. They used DNN and MLP models, two kinds of neural network. Tékouabou et al. (2022) [8] proposed ensemble models that combine different ways of handling data. They used machine learning models whose decisions can be explained, to improve churn prediction in banking.
parts.conclusion:
5 Conclusion and future work

In this section we sum up how our combined method works in practice, and we suggest future work for using it in real banking systems. We also add two short sections: one on acknowledgments and one on where to find our data.

5.1 Conclusion

To sum up, our combined SVC-SDNN model shows that deep learning can pick out useful patterns from data that go beyond what well-tuned tree-based and linear models can reach. This gives a big advantage for the important job of predicting churn. Our goal was to predict which bank customers would leave, and we focused on the SVC-SDNN model, which performed admirably.

After carefully preparing the data, we built and tested several models that sort customers into groups. These were Random Forest with Sequential Deep Neural Network (RF-SDNN), Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Sequential Deep Neural Network (SDNN). We judged them with scores such as F1-score, accuracy, precision and recall.

Of these, SVC-SDNN did best, with an accuracy of 95 percent and an AUC-ROC score of 0.881696. These results highlight its excellent prediction accuracy and its ability to tell churners and non-churners apart efficiently. Its precision, recall and F1-score were strong for both groups, which showed that the model is reliable. A confusion matrix is a table that shows how many customers of each kind the model got right and wrong. It showed in our experiments that the model correctly sorted non-churners and identified churners, with only a small number of mistakes.

The other models, RF-SDNN, SDNN, SVM and Random Forest, reached good accuracy levels of about 82 percent. However, they struggled to tell churners and non-churners apart, which gave them a lower AUC-ROC score. Their precision, recall and F1-score were also unbalanced, especially for the churner group [26].

5.2 Future work

This research can be extended in the following ways:

We should add more churner examples to the data, a technique called data augmentation, to even out the gap between the two groups, especially the churner group.

We should use the churn predictions to plan ways of keeping customers, such as personalized marketing campaigns and loyalty programs.

We should examine and discuss ethical questions about protecting customers' private data and about whether the model's predictions are fair.

We should focus on actually building the churn prediction model into banks' current systems.
parts.introduction_rest:
1.1 Why we did this research, and why it matters

Our combined method, SVC-SDNN, joins a Support Vector Classifier with a Sequential Deep Neural Network. We built it to predict churn in any dataset stored as a CSV file, the common spreadsheet format where each row is a customer and each column is a piece of information about them, such as their age or how much they spend. Predicting churn early brings many benefits to banks. Because we know the banking business well, we designed this model to sort customers into churners and non-churners.

Predicting churn has helped banks in several ways. It has improved their purchases, their income and their public relationships. It also helps with customer relationship management, which depends on keeping customers. Earlier methods of predicting churn have weaknesses: they take a long time and rely only on gut feelings about customers. Joining a Sequential Deep Neural Network with a Support Vector Machine can find loyal customers effectively [9]. This kind of AI method estimates how customers behave very precisely. In our case, the SVC-SDNN combination is specially aimed at predicting churn, and it helps us keep loyal customers. Bank staff can then feel more confident when they make decisions about how to look after their customers. Our research gives them a tool, and it helps them understand how customers behave. As a result, the share of customers that banks keep goes up.

In banking, churn prediction means spotting the customers who are likely to leave for a rival bank, so that the bank can act to keep them. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) and Support Vector Machines (SVMs) are two powerful machine learning methods, and each has its own strengths for this job. Using them together makes a business more valuable in a crowded market. Our method would help banks keep more customers and manage their relationships with them better. SVC-SDNN is more accurate at predicting which customers will stay. Because the combined approach is tailored to the particular dataset, it also makes fewer prediction mistakes.

Once churn is predicted accurately, a business can spend its money and effort more wisely. It can run marketing campaigns aimed at particular groups of people, or personalized for each customer. Banks can pay special attention to loyal customers, which leads to better customer service and a relationship people can trust. Knowing accurately how customers behave helps us make good plans for keeping them. Businesses then gain an edge over their rivals and always stay ahead in the market.

Our combined method, SVC-SDNN, focuses on one goal: predicting churn in banking datasets. To judge how well it works, we used four scores: accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score. We also compared it with another combined method, Random Forest with Sequential Deep Neural Network (RF-SDNN). We compared it with Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Sequential Deep Neural Network (SDNN) on their own as well. Better churn sorting also makes customers happier and helps more of them stay. AI-powered systems lead to efficient customer relationship management, with more profit and more success [10].

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. The Introduction sets the stage with background, our reasons for doing the research, the problem we set out to solve, our goals, why the study matters and what it covers. The Literature Review looks at recent research, focusing on Random Forests (RF) and Support Vector Machines (SVM), and explains the setting for that review [11]. The Research Methodology section describes how we collected the data, how we set up our computer experiments, how we prepared the data, how we split it into parts, and our proposed SVC-SDNN model. It also explains how the method is designed, how we chose its settings, and how we measured its performance. The Experimental Results section tests SVM and Random Forest on their own. It also tests the two combined models, SVC-SDNN (Support Vector Classifier + Sequential DNN) and RF-SDNN (Random Forest + Sequential DNN). This section sums up what we found and what each chapter shows. The Conclusion sums up the study and suggests future research, such as improving the combined models or trying new datasets.

The key points of this article are these. It uses combined models that join traditional sorting methods (SVM and RF) with deep learning (Sequential DNN) to get better results. It follows a clear, step-by-step process, paying close attention to preparing the data, splitting it and testing the models carefully. It is also practical, aiming to make predictions more accurate by creating a new method. Overall, it balances a review of theory, careful methods and real experiments to tackle the challenge of sorting customers into groups [12].
parts.methods:
3 Materials and methods

In this section we introduce our combined model, SVC-SDNN, and explain its main parts and how they fit together. We then describe how we trained the model and which settings affect how well it works. Finally, we explain the four scores we used to judge how well SVC-SDNN predicts churn: accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score.

Fig 4 shows the steps of our research. First we collected the data. Next we prepared it. Then we split it into two parts: a training set and a testing set. We used the training set to teach SVC-SDNN, and the testing set to check how well it worked. The four scores were part of this check. Our model's predictions of whether customers would stay were good [23].

Fig 4

The steps of our research, showing our combined approach.

Preparing the data came first and had three steps. Building the model came second and had two steps.

3.1 Where the data came from

We took our churn data from Kaggle, a website where people share data and code. The data is used to predict whether a bank customer will keep using the bank (US.Bank) or stop. For each customer, the data holds several important details, or features. Which features we choose affects how correctly churn can be predicted. In our case, age, balance, credit cards and credit score are very important for predicting churn precisely.

3.2 Looking at the data and preparing it

Table 2 describes the churn data. It holds 10,000 customer records and 12 columns of information. The records are numbered from 0 to 9999. The features we chose for predicting churn include customer information, financial details and the churn label itself.

The table shows that no values are missing. We also checked for repeated records using a command called DataFrame.duplicated().sum(), which counts how many records appear more than once. The answer was 0, so there were none. The original code and a screenshot of the output table are in our shared coding notebook. Table 2 shows the features, how many records have a value for each one, and what kind of data each feature holds.

Fig 5 shows how the balance is spread out in each group. For non-churners, the median balance is less than 100,000. The median is the middle value when all the values are lined up in order. For churners, the median is more than 100,000.

We also looked at the quartiles, which mark the points a quarter, half and three-quarters of the way along the line of values. For non-churners, the lowest value is Q1, the highest is around 225,000, and Q3 is about 130,000. For churners, the median is over 100,000, and Q1 is close to, and below, 50,000. Their Q3 is slightly higher than the Q3 of non-churners, and their lowest and highest values are 0 and 250,000. After this analysis, we prepared the data so that it would work well with machine learning and deep learning methods [24].

Fig 5

How the balance is spread out in the churn (1) and non-churn (0) groups.

We carried out several preparation steps. First, we turned categories into numbers, so that the methods could work with them. Second, we chose the features that have the biggest effect on the outcome [19]. The features we chose were 'balance', 'products_number', 'credit_score', 'credit_card', 'active_member', and the label 'churn'. These steps are essential for helping the models learn from the data and predict accurately. They also make sure the data is ready to be split and analysed.

3.3 Splitting the data

To predict churn, we split the data into two separate parts. We used 80% of it for training and kept the other 20% for testing. We used the training set to build and improve the model. We used the testing set to check how well the model worked and how accurate its predictions were.

Splitting the data like this lowers the risk of overfitting. Overfitting happens when a model learns the training examples too closely, including their quirks, and then does badly on new data. Keeping the two parts apart gives a fair test of how well the model handles data it has never seen. By "unseen data" we mean a private dataset with no missing or infinite values.

3.4 Balancing the data for churn prediction with deep neural networks

Our churn data was badly unbalanced. Only 7.2% of the customers were churners: 1,440 churners compared with 18,560 non-churners. When we first tried the model on this unbalanced data, it reached 92.8% accuracy. But its recall for the churn group was only 41.3%, meaning it found less than half of the real churners. That is clearly not good enough for a business, where spotting people who might leave matters most.

3.4.1 How we split and balanced the data

To make the test fair, we first split the whole dataset using a stratified split. This means the churners and non-churners were kept in the same proportions in both parts. This gave a training set of 80% (16,000 records) and a held-back test set of 20% (4,000 records). We set the test set aside and did not touch it at any point while training or balancing the model. This stopped any information from the test set from leaking into training, and it copied a realistic situation in which a model meets new customers.

To deal with the severe imbalance in the training data, we combined two ways of balancing. The first was to create new, made-up churn examples. The second was to adjust the model itself. We used a method called SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique) together with a method called Tomek Links, and we applied them only to the training set. SMOTE creates new churn examples that are similar to the real ones. Tomek Links removes borderline non-churner examples that sit close to churners and could confuse the model. Together, these gave us a balanced training set, with one churner example for every non-churner example, for building the model.

3.4.2 Balancing inside the model

For our combined SVC-SDNN model, we also gave each of its two parts a way to pay extra attention to the smaller group. We gave the Support Vector Classifier class weights that were inversely proportional to how common each group was in the original data. In other words, the rarer group got more weight.

The Stacked De-noising Neural Network used a custom loss function. A loss function is a score of how wrong the model's answers are, and the model learns by trying to make it smaller. Our loss function counted false negatives (missed churners) 2.3 times more heavily than false positives (false alarms). This reflects the cost a business pays when it misses a customer who is leaving.

Our experiments showed that this two-part approach worked better than either method on its own. All the scores we report, such as 79.4% recall and 72.1% precision for the churn group, come from testing the final model on the original, unbalanced test set of 4,000 records. This gives a true measure of how well it works on unseen, real-world data.

SMOTE alone raised the recall for churners to 68.2% on the validation set. Our combined approach did better, without losing precision: 72.1% compared with 65.3% for SMOTE. The whole system also kept good accuracy on the larger group, at 94.2%, while it greatly improved its ability to detect churners.

3.5 The SVC-SDNN model

Deep neural networks perform a convolution operation and are purely discriminative. This means they are built to tell groups apart, rather than to create new content. How well a deep neural network suits a particular dataset matters. Large language models, also called transformers, are an example of generative AI, which creates new content. For our churn data and its features, shown in Fig 6, an improved combined sequential deep neural network is the best choice.

Fig 6

Balance of the churn and non-churn groups, shown as a bar chart, a box chart, a violin plot and a statistical summary.

Each AI method is suited to certain situations and problems. This means that for every possible real-world problem there are several well-suited solutions. Some methods perform impressively on certain kinds of problems and certain datasets. Churn prediction can be done with discriminative AI, which tells groups apart. Large language models and generative AI work well in other areas.

We used a particular version of the Support Vector Classifier to sort customers into groups. The layered structure of the sequential deep neural network has been adjusted many times to improve how well it works. Our proposed SVC-SDNN model combines a Support Vector Classifier (SVC) with a Sequential Deep Neural Network (SDNN). It joins machine learning with deep learning.

The Support Vector Classifier is a particular version of the Support Vector Machine (SVM) used for sorting things into groups. It works by finding the best dividing boundary, called a hyperplane, that separates the data points into different groups. It can handle data that can be split by a straight line and data that cannot. It also makes the gap between the support vectors and the dividing boundary as wide as possible. Support vectors are the data points that sit closest to the boundary.

The Sequential Deep Neural Network (SDNN) is a powerful deep learning tool, and researchers are still developing it. Deep neural networks can handle complicated, non-linear links between inputs and outputs, such as spotting patterns and sorting things into groups (Bala & Kumar, 2017) [12].

Three key parts of a deep neural network are the dense layer, the optimizer and the loss function. A dense layer, also called a fully connected layer, is a part of a neural network in which each neuron is connected to every neuron in the layer before it [25]. It carries out a linear transformation of the input data and then applies an activation function to the output (Keras, 2022) [26]. An activation function is a simple rule that decides how strongly each neuron passes on its signal.

The optimizer plays a central role in making the loss function as small as possible. It does this by fine-tuning the weights and biases of the neurons in an artificial neural network (ANN). Weights and biases are the adjustable numbers inside the network. Well-known optimizers for ANNs include Adam, AdaGrad and stochastic gradient descent (SGD) [12]. SGD, for example, nudges the network step by step in the direction that lowers the loss.

The loss function measures the gap between the output the model expects and the ground truth, which is the correct answer. ANNs often use cross-entropy, binary cross-entropy and mean squared error (MSE) as loss functions (Yathish, 2022) [25]. Binary cross-entropy is a common choice when the model predicts yes or no.

3.6 Training the model and its important settings

Many settings can affect how well SVC-SDNN works. The important settings for the SVC are probability, class weight, gamma, kernel and C.

The C setting, also called the regularization setting, controls the balance between two goals. One is making as few mistakes as possible on the training data. The other is keeping the dividing boundary simple. A larger C tries to cut down training mistakes but may lead to overfitting. A smaller C allows a wider gap but may lead to more training mistakes.

The kernel decides what kind of boundary the SVC can draw. Common choices are the linear kernel, the polynomial kernel, the radial basis function (RBF) kernel and the sigmoid kernel (scikit-learn, 2023) [13]. The RBF kernel can draw curved boundaries. The gamma setting mainly affects the curved boundaries that kernels such as RBF produce. Giving the smaller group higher class weights lets the SVC pay it more attention during training. The probability setting lets the SVC estimate how likely each group is, based on the support vectors. This can help in some uses, such as calibrating the probabilities and choosing a cut-off for decisions (scikit-learn, 2023) [13].

We chose the RBF kernel for the Support Vector Classifier because it has a proven ability to model the complicated, non-linear links we expect in churn data. Its flexibility in capturing detailed patterns often makes it perform better than linear or polynomial kernels for this kind of problem, as earlier studies in financial analysis have also found.

The batch size is the number of training examples the model looks at in one go before it updates itself. A small batch size may take longer to reach a sensible answer. But it uses less memory and can work better on new cases (Brownlee, 2022) [27].

To avoid overfitting, we used batch normalization to check how well the model was doing during training. Batch normalization rescales the numbers passing through the network so that training stays steady. We set aside 10% of the training data for validation, with a validation split of 0.1, and used the other 90% to train the model (Agrawal, 2021) [28]. Fig 7 shows how the data was split into training and testing parts (Table 3).

Table 3

Settings (hyper-parameters) of the SVC-SDNN model and how to choose them.

| Setting | What it does | Typical values or options | How to choose it / what it does

| Support Vector Classifier (SVC) settings

| C | Regularization strength: the balance between training mistakes and the width of the gap. | 10⁻³, 10⁻², 10⁻¹, 1, 10, 100 (on a log scale) | Large C → low bias, risk of overfitting; small C → wider gap, higher bias. Choose by cross-validation.

| kernel | Kernel function: how the data is mapped into a space where it can be separated. | linear, poly, rbf (default), sigmoid | rbf works well for non-linear churn patterns; linear for data with many features that are mostly zero; poly for moderate non-linearity. Test each with cross-validation.

| gamma | Kernel coefficient for the rbf, poly and sigmoid kernels; controls the shape of the dividing boundary. | 'scale' (default), 'auto', or set values from 10⁻³ to 10¹ | Small γ → smoother, more overall boundary; large γ → tighter boundary, possibly overfitted. Adjust together with C.

| class_weight | Weights given to each group to handle imbalance. | None (default), 'balanced', or a dictionary, e.g., {0:1, 1:5} | Use 'balanced' or raise the weight of the smaller group by hand to improve recall on rare churners.

| probability | Switches on probability estimates using Platt scaling. | True/False (default) | Set to True when calibrated probabilities or a cut-off for decisions are needed; costs extra cross-validation.

| Deep Neural Network (SDNN) training settings

| batch_size | Number of examples handled before the model's weights are updated. | Small (16–32) → slower to settle, less memory; medium (64–128); large (256+) → faster but may work less well on new cases | Smaller batches often work better on new cases; choose based on GPU memory and training speed.

| validation_split | Share of the training data held back for checking each epoch (one full pass through the data). | 0.1 (10%) – default; can range from 0.05 to 0.2 | Gives a signal to stop training early and helps spot overfitting; keep enough data for training (at least 80%).

| batch_normalization | Rescales the numbers in each layer for each small batch to keep training steady. | On / off (usually on) | Helps with internal covariate shift (the network's own numbers drifting during training), helps training settle faster and reduces overfitting.

Fig 7

For the training data:

Xtrain′ = (Xtrain − μtrain) / σtrain (1)

For the test data:

Xtest′ = (Xtest − μtrain) / σtrain (2)

Here X is the data, μ is the average and σ is the spread. In words, we subtract the average of the training data from each value and divide by the spread of the training data. This puts all the features on the same scale.

Fig 8 shows the full workflow of our combined SVC-SDNN method for predicting churn. It follows the steps in order, from preparing the data, through building the model, to the final check.

Fig 8

The full workflow of our approach, showing every step.

3.6.1 Preparing the data.

First, we normalized, or standardized, the features. This means we put them all on the same scale.

Xtrain′ = StandardScaler(Xtrain), Xtest′ = StandardScaler(Xtest)

We then split the dataset into training and testing sets.

3.6.2 Building the sequential deep neural network to pick out features.

We set up a sequential deep neural network to learn hidden features. These are useful patterns that are not obvious at first. Given an input vector x ∈ ℝ^d with d features, the deep neural network (DNN) works as follows:

h1 = Drop0.7(σReLU(W1x + b1)), W1 ∈ ℝ^(128×d), b1 ∈ ℝ^128 (3)

h2 = Drop0.8(σReLU(W2h1 + b2)), W2 ∈ ℝ^(64×128), b2 ∈ ℝ^64 (4)

h3 = σReLU(W3h2 + b3), W3 ∈ ℝ^(32×64), b3 ∈ ℝ^32 (5)

y = FeatureLayer(h3) (6)

where:

σReLU(z) = max(0, z) is the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation function. It keeps positive values and turns negative values into zero.

Drop_p(·) is dropout regularization, which keeps each value with probability p (applied to each value separately during training). Dropout randomly switches off some neurons during training, so the network cannot lean too heavily on any one of them.

W_i and b_i are the weight matrix and bias vector for the i-th layer.

FeatureLayer(·) is the final step (it does nothing if nothing is specified).

We also set the number of epochs [29], the validation split and the batch size of the SDNN. An epoch is one full pass through the training data. Below we show the training and validation loss curves for the SDNN model. These curves show that the keep probabilities we chose (0.7 in the first hidden layer and 0.8 in the second) effectively prevent overfitting. The validation loss closely follows the training loss without drifting far apart, which shows that the model works very well on new data. Lower keep probabilities (for example, 0.5) led to underfitting, where the model was too simple to capture the data. Higher values (for example, 0.9) showed signs of overfitting on our particular dataset. Fig 9 shows the training of the combined SVC-SDNN model and the validation loss for each fold.

Fig 9

SVC-SDNN loss for each fold.

Training and validation loss for the ANN part of SVC-SDNN.

h1 = Drop0.7(σReLU(W1x + b1)) h2 = Drop0.8(σReLU(W2h1 + b2)) ... (7)

3.6.3 Pre-training the DNN (if processing power is available).

We added a classification head to the DNN. This is a final part that turns the hidden features into a yes-or-no answer. We pre-trained it on:

Xtrain′ = (Xtrain − μtrain) / σtrain (8)

Xtest′ = (Xtest − μtrain) / σtrain (9)

We trained it using binary cross-entropy:

ModelFull.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='binary_crossentropy') (10)

ModelFull.fit(X_train', y_train, epochs=50) (11)

We then removed the classification head to keep the hidden features. We used the DNN to turn the raw data into hidden features:

Xtrain_features = ModelDNN.predict(Xtrain) (12)

Xtest_features = ModelDNN.predict(Xtest) (13)

We trained the Support Vector Classifier (SVC). We set it up with the RBF kernel:

ModelSVC = SVC(kernel='rbf', C=1.0, gamma='scale') (14)

We fitted the SVC on the features picked out by the DNN:

ModelSVC.fit(Xtrain_features, ytrain) ModelSVC.fit(Xtrain_features, ytrain) (15)

We checked the combined model by making predictions on the test data:

ytest = ModelSVC.predict(Xtest_features) ytest = ModelSVC.predict(Xtest_features) (16)

We calculated the performance scores:

(Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)) (17)

(F1 = 2PrecisionRecall / (Precision + Recall)) (18)

Here TP (true positives) are churners correctly found, TN (true negatives) are non-churners correctly found, FP (false positives) are false alarms, and FN (false negatives) are missed churners.

For fine-tuning, we joined the DNN and SVC into a single pipeline that can be trained together (advanced). The loss function can be customized, for example with hinge loss for the SVC. The errors from the SVC can then be passed back through the DNN using gradient approximation, a way of estimating how to adjust the DNN to reduce the errors.

3.6.4 Confusion matrix.

A confusion matrix is a two-dimensional table used to judge how well a method sorts things into groups. Fig 10 shows the normalized confusion matrix for SVC-SDNN. It has four basic parts: true positives (TP), true negatives (TN), false positives (FP) and false negatives (FN). We used the confusion matrix to calculate the scores that fully judge how well the model sorts customers: accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score.

Fig 10

Normalized confusion matrix for SVC-SDNN.

3.6.5 AUC-ROC score.

The AUC-ROC score measures how well a model tells the positive group (churners) apart from the negative group (non-churners). A perfect model scores 1.0, and a model that guesses at random scores 0.5.
parts.results:
4 Results

In this section we compare how well the different models performed, using several different scores. To make the results easier to see, we also use tables and confusion matrices.

4.1 How well the models performed

We tested four machine learning models [30]. The first was the Support Vector Classifier with Sequential Deep Neural Network (SVC-SDNN). The second was Random Forest with Sequential Deep Neural Network (RF-SDNN). The third was the Sequential Deep Neural Network (SDNN) on its own. The fourth was the Support Vector Machine (SVM) on its own.

To judge how well each model sorted customers into groups, we used five scores: accuracy, AUC-ROC, precision, recall and F1-score. A confusion matrix shows how well a model tells the churner group and the non-churner group apart. Together, these scores made it easier to see the strengths and weaknesses of each model for keeping customers.

Table 4 compares the accuracy and AUC-ROC of SVC-SDNN, SDNN, Random Forest, SVC and RF-SDNN. SVC-SDNN had the highest accuracy (0.95) and the highest AUC-ROC (0.8817), and it clearly beat the other models. RF-SDNN, SDNN and SVM had similar accuracy (0.82), but their AUC-ROC scores differed: 0.6138, 0.5651 and 0.5531. Random Forest had slightly lower accuracy (0.79), but its AUC-ROC (0.6141) was higher than that of SDNN and SVM.

These results show that SVC-SDNN is robust. Compared with the next-best model, its accuracy was 12.8% higher and its AUC-ROC was 44% higher.

Many banks prefer cloud services, which are easier and safer to use. Predicting churn in a cloud environment is also fairly easy [31]. However, a churn prediction product that banks want to run in real time needs advanced, improved chip technology. Fitting any suitable method onto a modern chip needs help from experts in microprocessors [32].

4.3 What the comparison tells us

How well any AI model that sorts things into groups performs depends on the number and kind of features, or attributes, used for loyal customers. To help banks look after their customers better, we tested how well several machine learning models sorted customers into groups.

The Support Vector Classifier with Sequential Deep Neural Network (SVC-SDNN) stood out. Its 95 percent accuracy and its AUC-ROC of 0.881696 showed excellent prediction accuracy and a strong ability to tell the groups apart. Its classification report showed high precision, recall and F1-score for both the non-churner and churner groups, which further showed its strength. Its confusion matrix confirmed that it sorted non-churners correctly and found churners, with only a few mistakes.

Random Forest, RF-SDNN, SDNN and SVM performed at different levels. Their AUC-ROC results were less impressive, which shows they had trouble telling the churner and non-churner groups apart. Even so, they reached similar accuracy levels of about 82 percent. Their precision, recall and F1-score were unbalanced, especially for the churner group. Random Forest reached an accuracy of 79 percent and had limits in telling the groups apart, with lower precision and recall for churners.

Our study focuses on traditional, sequential deep-learning models. Still, it is very relevant to explore other designs, such as Transformers and other attention-based methods, which are models that learn to focus on the most important parts of the data. These models have reached the best results so far in areas with complicated data that has many features, such as natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision [34]. Using them on table data, including for predicting customer churn, is an active area of research.

However, recent studies suggest that these models are not always the best. Table data is usually not ordered in time and mixes different kinds of features, such as numbers and categories. For this kind of data, well-tuned gradient-boosting machines (GBMs), such as XGBoost or LightGBM, often beat complicated deep learning models [35,36]. A GBM builds many simple decision trees one after another, with each new tree fixing the mistakes of the ones before it. Transformers are also known for needing huge amounts of data. They need very large datasets to show their full power without over-fitting, which is when a model memorizes its training examples instead of learning general patterns [37]. Most commercial churn prediction datasets are fairly small, often in the range of 10–4 samples 10–5. For data of this size, our ensemble and combined SVC-SDNN approach gives a sturdier solution that needs fewer adjustable settings. It avoids the heavy computing and the risk of over-fitting that come with running large attention-based models on such data [38].

Evolutionary computation, especially genetic algorithms, takes every possible answer into account to get precise results. It can be left out when a lightweight version of the model is needed [39]. Our analysis confirms that personal details (age) and money-related details (balance, credit score and card use) strongly affect churn predictions.

4.4 Checking our proposed method

Churn is a serious threat to how managers make decisions, and it harms customer relationship management. Running a marketing campaign aimed at a large number of churn customers wastes time and money. Efficient, effective smart AI solutions improve management decisions and investment. Combined models like SVC-SDNN beat pure attention-based methods on table data with a moderate number of features, because they balance accuracy with being practical to use. We recognize this limitation and point to it as a direction for future research, for cases with data that comes in several types or has a very large number of features over time.

4.5 Thorough testing and statistical significance

A calibration plot checks how well the probabilities that a model predicts match what really happened. This is crucial for judging how reliable a model is when it gives probabilities. Fig 9 shows calibration plots for each model (RF, SVM, ANN, RF-SDNN and SVC-SDNN). For each model, the plot compares the predicted probabilities with the true probabilities across 10 bins, or ranges, during the final round of stratified k-fold cross-validation (Tables 9 and 10). In this kind of testing, the data is split into several parts, and each model is tested on a different part each time, so that every group is fairly represented.

A perfectly calibrated model would follow the dashed diagonal line, where the predicted probability equals the true probability. The plot shows how far each model's curve moves away from this ideal line. Curves above the diagonal mean the model is under-confident, so its predictions are too low. Curves below the diagonal mean it is over-confident, so its predictions are too high.

This matters especially for churn prediction, where accurate probabilities are essential for making decisions. It shows not only whether a model can tell the groups apart, but also how well its predicted probabilities match the true chances. We can compare the calibration of the combined model directly with that of the models it is built from, to see whether combining them makes the probabilities more reliable as well as improving other scores.
